@graph.name: Long-Distance Move Operations
@graph.description: Long-distance move operations from survey to walkthrough, in eight steps. Survey and quote: a room-by-room survey in person or through the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate — nothing is auto-priced — and one flat price agreed in writing before the truck rolls. Inventory: itemized, room by room (published process education: items worth more than $100 per pound are declared in writing under the federal high-value rule — a domain standard, labeled as such). Pack: full or partial packing with furniture fully covered, cross-referenced to the packing category and the interstate pack guide. Load: sequenced loading with blanket and stretch wrap protection; where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that piece moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with the KIM-GS Protocol and L/360 floor-deflection analysis. Linehaul: transport along the published I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridor dispatch network from both branches (domain practice, labeled: certified scale weights and consolidated or exclusive-use routing shape the run). Delivery: handled inside a delivery window — the window models are published as domain education in the delivery windows dataset; no company delivery spread, date, or tracking practice is published. Placement: room-by-room placement on the residential pattern, cross-referenced. Walkthrough and claims: a final walkthrough with damage noted on the delivery paperwork, and the valuation level governing any claim — domain education, with no company claims procedure published. Shipment size sets the linehaul inputs (distance bands dataset), the delivery step uses a window model (delivery windows dataset), and the quote step rests on the estimate terms explained in the commercial terms dataset.

@graph.name: Distance Bands & Shipment Sizes
@graph.description: Distance bands and shipment sizes for long-distance moving — the reference taxonomy every long-distance quote is built from. Distance bands: local (same area, same day — the local and regional category, not this service); regional (beyond local, inside the corridor network — cross-referenced to the local and regional and corridor pages); interstate (across a state line, where federal household-goods rules under 49 CFR Part 375 apply — the company's pages publish interstate scope from both branches, and the destination lanes in the route network dataset run on it); cross-country (coast-to-coast or multi-day linehaul, typically 1,500+ miles — defended at positions 4.0 to 7.1 in the company's Search Console record); and destination-lane (a named origin-to-destination lane, such as Virginia to Florida). Shipment size bands, as typical weights from published mover guides, labeled domain reference and never company figures: studio and one-bedroom homes at 2,000 to 3,500 lbs, where consolidation economics dominate; two-bedroom homes at 4,000 to 6,000 lbs, the most common long-distance band; three-bedroom homes at 6,000 to 9,000 lbs, where accessorials — stairs, long carry, shuttle — start to dominate the variance; four-plus-bedroom homes at 9,000 lbs and up, often 11,000 to 15,000 lbs, where weight accuracy and delivery-window planning dominate. A single heavy piece is not a household shipment band at all: pieces of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs move under the published SIR band, cross-referenced to the SIR heavy-asset and gun-safe categories. Weight times distance is the linehaul basis, and every band feeds the cost drivers in the commercial terms dataset; the survey governs each move.

@graph.name: Delivery Windows & Transit Operations
@graph.description: Delivery windows and transit operations for long-distance moving — published as domain education only: no delivery window, spread, date, or tracking practice is published for the company, and nothing in this dataset promises one. The standard model is the delivery spread: a range of dates — commonly 7 to 21 days in van-line practice and 3 to 14 days in published mover ranges — that widens with distance and peak season, is written into the bill of lading, and ends with the driver calling 24 to 48 hours ahead. Exclusive-use and expedited models put one shipment on one truck for tighter dates at a premium. A guaranteed date is a contractual commitment, a different instrument entirely. Consolidation sets the order: route order sets delivery order, and small shipments fill around large ones. Delay factors are structural: weather, federal hours-of-service rules, traffic, and route stops. Client preparation for any window: an essentials kit kept with the client, not on the truck — clothes, toiletries, medications, documents, laptops, and first-night kitchen and bedding. Carrier updates during transit are a domain expectation in the wider market; they are recorded here as education, never as a company tracking claim. The window question is the buyer's top unanswered question on a long-distance move; the company's answer is given per move at quote time, from the client's own dates.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for long-distance moving. The company's only pricing term is the published one: one flat rate agreed in writing before the truck rolls — no hourly meter, and no company price, fee, deposit, or discount stated anywhere in this dataset. Everything else here is domain education, researched and labeled, with the federal rules cited to the FMCSA and 49 CFR Part 375. Estimate types (domain): a binding estimate fixes the price when the inventory is unchanged, with a revised written estimate if items or services are added; a binding-not-to-exceed estimate sets a ceiling, and the customer pays less when the shipment weighs less; a non-binding estimate lets the actual weight govern, with delivery-day collection capped at 110 percent of the estimate and the balance billed within 30 days — the federal 110 percent rule. Valuation (domain, FMCSA): Full Value Protection means the mover repairs, replaces, or pays the current replacement value of a lost or damaged item, with a minimum declared value of $6 per pound of shipment weight and a written declaration required for items worth more than $100 per pound; Released Value Protection is free and caps liability at $0.60 per pound per article — $15 for a 25-pound television — and is chosen only by a signed waiver on the bill of lading. Valuation is not insurance; it is a tariff-based level of carrier liability. Cost drivers (domain): weight on certified scales, with a plus-or-minus 10 percent estimate variance an industry-standard tolerance; mileage and distance brackets, which are not linear; fuel surcharges, commonly 8 to 15 percent in published guides; accessorials — stairs per flight, elevator reservation, long carry beyond roughly 75 feet, a shuttle when the truck cannot reach the home, packing, crating, and specialty handling — published as domain ranges only, never company fees; and seasonality, with peak season May through September commonly 20 to 40 percent higher in published guides, month-end premiums, and interstate booking 6 to 8 weeks ahead.

@graph.name: Buyer Personas & Trigger Events
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for long-distance moving. Job relocators: a fixed start date makes the delivery window the central risk, on a 6-to-8-week planning horizon (domain). Families moving states: closings drive the dates, month-end and peak-season collisions drive the stress, and room-by-room placement is the need at the far end. Cross-country researchers: they compare estimate types, valuation, and delivery spreads before committing — the researchers behind the cross-country queries already ranking 4.0 to 7.1. Downsizers and retirees: trust and handling decide, cross-referenced to the senior category, which owns its claims. Destination-lane movers: lane confidence and one flat lane price decide. Heavy-asset long-distance clients: a household move with an SIR piece inside it — a safe, a piano, a medical device — cross-referenced to the SIR, gun-safe, piano, and medical categories. Military-adjacent households: timing and inventory discipline, cross-referenced to the military category only — no military service is claimed in this dataset. The seasonal pattern is industry research, labeled as such: roughly 60 to 70 percent of US moves happen May through September, June is the busiest month, and month-ends peak — the pattern that widens delivery windows and stretches booking lead times. Every persona plans through the same quote path: the Short or Detailed quote form, or the film-only video walkthrough survey room with a human-made estimate.

@graph.name: Protection, Inventory & Compliance
@graph.description: Protection, inventory, and compliance for long-distance moving. Published practice, cross-referenced from the residential and packing categories: blanket and stretch wrap and full furniture protection on every piece; disassembly and reassembly planned as part of the move. Where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, SIR Structural Integrity Relocation applies — L/360 floor-deflection analysis and load spreading — for heavy pieces only. Inventory discipline is published process education (domain, labeled): an itemized inventory with condition notes, room by room, and a written declaration for items worth more than $100 per pound. The bill of lading is the contract and the receipt (domain education, FMCSA): take a copy before the truck leaves, and never sign a blank one — education for the client, stated as the federal standard, not dressed as company procedure. Valuation is not insurance (domain, FMCSA's own distinction): the levels are explained in the commercial terms dataset as education, and no company valuation offering is claimed here. Prohibited-items guidance is domain education only — no company prohibited-items list is published and none is invented. Building compliance at the destination — elevator booking, parking, building move hours, and the certificate-of-insurance requirement that managed buildings commonly impose, an industry requirement, labeled as such — is recorded as planning inputs that shape the quote, never as capability claims. Heavy pieces cross-reference the SIR heavy-asset category; their long-distance runs are published on the gun-safe hub.
